title: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots
description: President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR)
body: President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) shots."Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today," Trump said on Monday. "In those times, people were much healthier and of course the high rates of autism now observed did not exist."The president has long cast doubt on the safety of MMR vaccines, but multiple studies have found no connection between the shots and autism.The order also recommends that the number of childhood vaccines drop to 11 from the existing 18 recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump said that his administration "is recognising gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases".The immunisations recommended for all children under the order are for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella or chicken pox."We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor."The president suggested that the MMR vaccine could be "quite lethal" if given at once. He compared it to pouring a bottle of soda into a child's body.Experts say that allowing time between jabs means children are more likely to contract diseases in the interim or that they are more likely to miss appointments if there are multiple shots.According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, external (CDC), there is "no published scientific evidence that shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots". The agency says "most people who get MMR vaccine do not have any serious problems with it", and that getting the vaccine "is much safer than getting measles, mumps, or rubella".Trump's Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F Kennedy Jr said the proposed changes were meant to give parents choice, not prohibit access to childhood vaccines.The federal government does not have the authority to implement the new recommendations. Shots that are required for school attendance are set at the state level.Dr Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, called Trump's executive order "disheartening" and "dangerous", pointing out it comes as measles cases reach a 35-year high in the US. Measles cases have also been rising globally. "Instead of ensuring every family can access life-saving vaccines for measles, influenza, RSV and more, federal leaders are once again spreading misleading claims," Racine said in a statement on Monday.He said there was no new evidence to justify the significant changes, adding that the order was not based on "gold-standard science"."Delaying or skipping shots is risky, especially as measles continues to spread and children go back to school," Racine said. Republican Senator Bill Cassidy also admonished Trump's executive order on Monday, labelling it "wrong"."The President does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy, who is a physician, wrote on social media. "Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism."The lawmaker, who chairs the Senate health committee, urged parents to "listen to their child's pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order". Experts fear that if parents refrain from getting their children vaccinated as a result of the discredited idea that childhood vaccines are linked to autism, it risks the re-emergence of diseases like measles.Multiple studies have found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism. A recent high-quality study from Denmark in 2019 looked at 657,461 children and concluded that the data did not support the MMR vaccine causing or triggering autism.On its website, the US CDC recommends that two doses of the combined MMR vaccine be given to children, starting with the first dose at 12-15 months and the second between the ages of four and six.How often and how many vaccines children in the US receive is based on the times when vaccines will work best with their immune systems and when they are most vulnerable to certain diseases, according to the AAP.There is no medical reason to delay or skip recommended immunisations, the AAP says.

schema.headline: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots

title: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJessica RawnsleyThe world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJessica RawnsleyThe world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific, according to the EU's climate monitoring service.The average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the world's polar regions - between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south - was 20.96C last month, beating the previous high of 20.89C, set in 2023.Last month was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.Meanwhile, Western Europe experienced its hottest ever June and July, with prolonged hot and dry conditions fuelling extreme wildfires across the region.Elsewhere, the UK is braced for its fifth heatwave of the year this week, as persistent dry weather puts further pressure on water supplies and could see more areas officially declared in drought.Around Europe, sea surface temperatures in July reached record highs along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread strong and severe marine heatwaves.Sea temperatures remained exceptionally high across much of the tropical Pacific, where El Niño conditions are developing and forecast to strengthen in the coming months. El Niño is a natural weather pattern in the Pacific that combined with human-driven global warming can cause temperature spikes and more extreme weather.Oceans are a vital regulator of the climate, absorbing most of the excess heat generated by greenhouse gas emissions and producing half of Earth's oxygen.The greatest effect of ocean warming is on sea level rise. As seawater warms it expands, and this thermal expansion accounts for roughly a third of sea level rise recorded by scientists to date. That water encroaches on low-lying coasts and island nations.Hotter seas are also driving longer and fiercer marine heatwaves, which have bleached coral reefs on a mass scale and decimated kelp forests and fisheries.Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, intensifying tropical storms and loading them with heavier rainfall.'Climate change is intensifying heat extremes'Western Europe is experiencing an exceptional run of extreme heat - with record-breaking temperatures in June and July, and some areas facing their third or fourth heat wave since May.The average temperature across western Europe for June and July was 21.62C - 2.79C above average and the highest for the two-month period."July 2026 was the third consecutive month of exceptional heat in western Europe," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over the region, she said, while dry soils reduced the ability to provide natural cooling."This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another," she added.France, Spain, parts of Germany and the UK recorded exceptionally low rainfall and/or soil moisture, while soil moisture levels across much of western Europe were significantly lower than in 2022, when the region experienced severe drought.River levels have been much lower than average - in some places exceptionally low -with the Seine, Rhine and Danube among those particularly affected.Low flows exacerbate pressure on water supplies and irrigation, aquatic ecosystems, river transport and energy production.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Some rivers in Europe have recorded extremely low water levels, including the Danube The prolonged hot and dry conditions have created favourable conditions for wildfires, with massive wildfires raging across western Europe last month and "exceptional activity" in terms of the area burned and smoke and emissions generated."Climate change is increasingly bringing the kinds of hot and dry conditions that favour large, high-intensity wildfires in southern Europe while extended the fire season northwards," said Laurence Rouil, director of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.Larger fires produce more smoke and inject it higher into the atmosphere, allowing it to travel much further, he said.That means countries that experience relatively few wildfires could be increasingly affected by smoke traveling long distances.Extreme weather 'new normal'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, European wildfires haven been called "completely unprecedented" this summerIn the UK, meanwhile, the prolonged dry spell is increasing pressure on already-stretched water supplies.England and Wales recorded their driest July since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, while large parts of England and all of Wales have already been officially declared in drought.The Environment Agency has warned that more areas of England could be declared in drought if dry conditions persist.Weather that was once considered extreme is becoming the "new normal", according to the latest Met Office report on the UK's climate.Its latest assessment found that the hottest day of the year in southern England is now 4.5C warmer than it was between 1961 and 1990."We are right now living in a time of historic and unprecedented change," said Mike Kendon, Met Office climate information scientist, adding that "evidence shows the climate of the 20th century has now gone".Scientists say El Niño may temporarily push global temperatures even higher. Its effects are being felt against a backdrop of man-made warming, particularly the burning of fossil fuels.The world is now about 1.4C warmer on average than it was in the late 19th Century.

schema.headline: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures

title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
description: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on
body: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers -  the case that Mathipa had been investigating.After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.Outside the UK watch on YouTube, externalThe case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks. Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer."When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.

schema.headline: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC

title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
description: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?A major drive
body: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a €150,000 (£128,000) fine, if convicted.Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Étape forest in the Vosges region. "Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est Républicain, the newspaper that reported the story.Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts."I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances. "The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying. Working out how a fire started is, unsurprisingly, not easy."In periods of drought such as this one, all you need is a simple lighter," explains Eric Dufayet, an officer who investigates fires.Once a fire is out, Eric's first task is to map its outline along the edge of the burnt vegetation, then trace it back to its point of origin. If the wind has been steady, that outline often forms a "V" shape. From there, his team works backwards along the path the flames took."If someone deliberately starts a fire, they may not have used only one device," he says. It improves the chances of a DNA or fingerprint sample being found.Experts believe arson accounts for only a small fraction of fires. Most are believed to be accidental, with sparks potentially coming from construction work, faulty electrical equipment, cigarette butts and barbecues."With cigarettes, it's called the '30' rule," says Eric Dufayet. To start a fire, he explains, there must be "a temperature of at least 30C (86F), a maximum of 30% humidity, wind of less than 30km/h (19mph), and at least 30% of the cigarette unburnt."In the current drought, he says it is even easier. If those conditions are met, a fire can easily spread, and fast.According to Michel Lejoyeux, a professor of psychiatry and addictive behaviour at Paris 7 University, people who start fires fall into three categories: those who are careless, those who benefit - with an insurance payout, for example - and pyromaniacs."The pyromaniac doesn't get money, has no spirit of revenge, has no utility of the fire, but he likes the fire," he says.However, pyromania is a rare psychiatric disorder that Lejoyeux says is very difficult to diagnose, and accounts for few arson convictions.Lawyer Muriel Gestas, who has handled several such cases, says some firefighters alleged to have started fires may have wanted to be seen as saviours. For others - notably volunteers earning tax-free overtime - the motive may be financial.Amid concerns over how officials are pursuing suspects, broader worries about wildfires are far from abating. Forecasts suggest France's next heatwave is only days away.President Emmanuel Macron says criticism should not be the priority right now. "We will have to replant and rebuild a different kind of forest because we must adapt to the structural conditions of climate change," he said this week."The time for reviewing lessons learned will come," he insisted. "In the meantime, the country must remain united."Even so, the damage these fires have inflicted on the environment, hundreds of homes, tourism, local businesses and air quality has left the French public with a lot of questions.

schema.headline: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?

title: 'We've had a lot of close calls': Canada wildfire evacuees wonder if they still have homes
description: Figure caption, "That fire came so fast": Wildfire rages in British ColumbiaByNadine YousifSenior Canada reporter and Brandon DrenonBBC NewsEarl Kurz
body: Figure caption, "That fire came so fast": Wildfire rages in British ColumbiaByNadine YousifSenior Canada reporter and Brandon DrenonBBC NewsEarl Kurz and his wife have lived in Peachland, a town overlooking Okanagan Lake in Canada's British Columbia, for 30 years. In the last 10, he said he has grown used to wildfires threatening his community.But this is the first time he's been forced to flee, and surveying the damage left behind by the Bald Range wildfire, which broke out on Friday and grew in a matter of hours to 53 sq miles (136 sq km) in size, has been difficult."It's total incinerated destruction," Kurz said. "The hot spots are just barren areas of nothing except 12 inches of ash."Officials in British Columbia are still trying to determine how many homes were lost to the fire, which remains out of control as of Monday. More than 12,000 residents in the area are still under an evacuation order. One woman, aged 80, died while trying to flee from the wildfire, police said on Sunday.With dry lightning, high temperatures and winds in the forecast, officials warned on Monday that the fire continues to be a threat and that new ignitions are possible.The Okanagan area of British Columbia, known for its world renowned vineyards and picturesque scenery, has been grappling with extreme drought in recent years. As of July, the level of the Okanagan Lake was at its lowest since 1992, according to the Okanagan Basin Water Board.The Bald Range wildfire is one of more than 100 burning in British Columbia as of Monday - 70 of which started in the last week alone. The west coast province's premier, David Eby, declared a state of emergency over the weekend, urging residents to heed evacuation orders and warning that the fires continue to move "incredibly quickly".Image source, Supplied/Keegan RadomskiImage caption, Keegan Radomski's home, photographed here before the fire, was built by her grandmother in 1996. Keegan Radomski is one of thousands who have had to flee their homes in Summerland, a town on the Okanagan Lake just south of Peachland. The 18-year-old told the BBC she barely escaped with her mother's ashes before she saw the fire breach her property."We've had a lot of close calls before, but it's never been like this," Radomski said. "You always think it's not going to be you, and then it's you."The home she fled was built by her grandmother 30 years ago, she said. Living in the Okanagan for decades meant that Radomski and her family are familiar with wildfires and evacuation notices, but they were still caught off guard by the speed of this fire. The family noticed wildfire smoke from the distance while eating dinner on Friday evening. Less than four hours later, Radomski said she was scrambling to get everyone out as she saw a hill on her property begin to burn. She added she is still unsure if her family's home survived, and when she can return and check for herself.Image source, Supplied by Keegan RadomskiImage caption, Radomski says she is unsure of when she is able to return to her property and assess the damageDoug Holmes, the mayor of Summerland, told CBC News on Monday that some people's homes have been lost, but "we don't know how many"."I think we need to prepare for the fact that everybody is going to know somebody that has lost a home," Holmes said.Some residents in the farming community were forced to leave their livestock behind in the quick evacuation, said Kaz Nowlin, who has been helping rescue stranded animals in the Okanagan area since wildfires broke out last month. Nowlin said he and a group of volunteers have so far rescued dozens of animals, including 57 horses. He told the BBC he is in the process of acquiring a permit to enter Summerland and round up 14 alpacas and eight horses that have remained. "It's for the animals' well-being," he said of his efforts. "They don't deserve what's going on."Image source, Supplied by Kaz NowlinImage caption, Dozens of horses have been rescued by a volunteer group in and around the Okanagan Valley since wildfires broke out last month. The Bald Range wildfire comes on the heels of another fire in the Okanagan, called Bradley Creek, which is believed to have destroyed more than 200 homes.Officials said the Bradley Creek fire is now being held after "tireless work" by wildfire crews to contain it. Drought conditions have also contributed to fires in the US state of Washington, just south of British Columbia, where more than 65,000 people were forced to flee their homes. Devastating fires have also burned this summer in Spain and France as Europe grapples with drought and record high temperatures. France has seen its worst fires in two decades, while officials in the Spanish capital Madrid say theirs are the worst the region has ever experienced.Fires are part of the natural cycle of Canada's vast boreal forest, but experts say climate change - particularly hotter and dryer weather - has made them more intense and frequent in the last decade. In 2023, the country saw its worst wildfire season in history in terms of the total area burned.

schema.headline: 'We've had a lot of close calls': Canada wildfire evacuees wonder if they still have homes

title: Nigeria's mass wedding - and how to tell lovers from fraudsters in Kano
description: Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass
body: Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding.For days the city's streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events.On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went to the palace of the Emir, the city's traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife.The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds.The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot - providing the bride's dowry and furniture for the couple's first home.The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage.The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples - primarily widows and divorcees - wed at the palace.The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages.Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year.The event is always overseen by the Hisbah - the city's Islamic police force - and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed.Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system.Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task."Whenever we find out that there's something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them," he tells the BBC.He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer.The state government has spent approximately 1m naira ($735; £544) on each participating couple.According to the Hisbah, the support package a couple receives includes essential household items needed to establish a new home: beds, mattresses, bedsheets, pillows, furniture and food supplies.Each bride receives a dowry of 100,000 naira, while a further 100,000 naira is provided as start-up capital to encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and help the couple achieve financial self-reliance after marriage.All intending couples must undergo comprehensive medical examinations - including tests for HIV, hepatitis, pregnancy and genotype compatibility - before being cleared for the programme.Aminudeen revealed that some couples had been disqualified after being discovered to have altered their medical test results.In one case, an intending bride was found to have presented her brother as the groom in an attempt to benefit from the scheme.Local journalist Yusuf Ali Abdallah, who has covered the mass weddings for years, said Nigeria's struggling economy had been fuelling desperation among the applicants this year."As we all know, marriage involves spending money and the country's economy is not bright at the moment," he told the BBC."This makes some people desperate to get on this list."One couple who were already married had even attempted to present themselves as an intending pair before being detected and removed from the programme, he said.Other charlatans have tried to take advantage of those desperate to get on the sponsored list, which was made public two weeks ago.One Kano resident, who asked to be anonymous, said he had been asked to pay a bribe to get on the list."But to be fair to the organisers, I later found out those who asked me for money were not Hisbah staff," he said.He and his fiancée failed to be chosen for this August's wedding but he said he would try again next year.Aminudeen admitted that the Islamic police were aware of such allegations: "We have found that there are some people asking others to pay certain money so they can make the list."But the Hisbah officer wanted to assure all those wishing to wed in future that the entire process should not cost them a single naira."We want to announce to the people of Kano that the whole process is free: from the selection to the medicals and the goods set aside for couples - all are covered by the government."One of successful grooms, 43-year-old clothes trader Rabiu Yusuf, agreed the process of applying to be married had gone smoothly for him."Personally, no-one asked me for anything. I was told the government would sponsor it all," he told the BBC.His new wife is Aisha Auwal - the couple met as she regularly visited his shop to buy clothes.Yusuf, who already has five children with his first wife, said he was "very happy and can't wait to start a new life" with his customer-turned-bride.24 year-old Amina Alhassan echoed his sentiments, adding that she had not encountered any problems when applying to marry 40-year-old Nura Abdullahi.Their union was first arranged by their families in Dambatta village before they presented themselves to the Hisbah."Everything has been free and I want to commend the Kano government for this scheme because without it, many couldn't have afforded to marry due to the high cost of living."After Saturday's wedding feast, the presentation of the household goods began.But it will take several more days for the excitement to die down in Kano and as the newlyweds busy themselves with setting up home together.

schema.headline: Nigeria's mass wedding - and how to tell lovers from fraudsters in Kano

title: Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word
description: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is unlikel
body: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is unlikely to be the final word.The White House is reportedly "not bothered" by Netanyahu's statement and views it as campaign rhetoric in the run-up to a heated general election."We understand Bibi's political needs" the Israeli journalist, Barak Ravid, quotes a senior US official as saying – using a nickname to refer to the Israeli leader. "We have no problem with it as long as he continues to do what we ask – especially regarding restraining attacks in Gaza."Recent days have seen an apparent pause in Israel's strikes on Gaza – something Hamas had demanded when signing on to the US-backed, 15-point roadmap.And there is another suggestion that Israel is ready to advance US President Donald Trump's peace plan for Gaza – getting ready for the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF). The force is made up of international troops, with the plan being for them to work with a new Palestinian police force to secure the territory.The expected construction of the first ISF base is still scheduled to begin amid the ruins of Rafah in southern Gaza at the end of this month, according to Israeli public radio, Kan News, which would allow reconstruction to begin at last.In July, after months of delicate negotiations, Trump announced a "major milestone" in the implementation of his plan to end Israel's war in Gaza. Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups in the territory.The deal is meant to be carried out in phases, with all weapons decommissioned and stored by a new Palestinian administration in Gaza – which reports to the Board of Peace - and Israeli forces withdrawing from the more than 60% of Gaza they currently control.Senior Hamas officials confirmed that they had agreed to the new framework, conditioning it on mutual compliance by Israel. This was widely viewed as a major potential breakthrough in the conflict. The UK welcomed it and the European Union hailed it as a "crucial step".However, for more than a week, Israel did not give its formal response. An Israeli spokesman said only that the roadmap did not "reflect Israel's positions." A far-right member of the government, Itamar Ben-Gvir, wrote on X that the deal was "unacceptable."Increasingly, mainstream Israeli opposition politicians also raised doubts. They questioned whether all small arms would be decommissioned and the sequencing of the plan.Finally on Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet, "I wish to be precise here: Israel does not accept the 15-point document."He added: "The IDF [Israel Defense Forces] will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament."In the same statement, the prime minister described President Trump as "the greatest of our friends in the White House" but said that Israel knew "how to stand firm" against unacceptable ideas.In Israel, there is widespread scepticism that Hamas intends to follow through on its commitments. The Islamist movement has long seen "armed struggle" as a core precept, its legitimate response to Israeli occupation of Palestinian lands. In recent months, there had been signs of it reasserting its authority in Gaza."Israel can certainly never agree to retreating anywhere where the terrorist group that caused the worst massacres since the Holocaust is still there and is still ruling the Strip," Fleur Hassan-Nahoum, an Israeli commentator and former deputy mayor of Jerusalem told the BBC.She stressed that the "trauma of the Israeli people" from the deadly Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, which ignited the devastating Gaza war, should not be underestimated.Any potential concessions for Netanyahu would come at a politically sensitive moment. He is facing an uphill contest in the upcoming general election, scheduled for 27 October. It will be Israel's first since the 7 October assault and three years on, Netanyahu has failed to secure what he vowed: "absolute victory" over Hamas.The former American diplomat and veteran Middle East negotiator, Aaron David Miller, said the Israeli leader is facing "the most consequential election" of his political life. "He's navigating a very fine line between keeping his constituents happy and not angering or alienating President Trump," he told the BBC.For now, he believes the White House recognises the situation and is giving Netanyahu "a pass."  Miller added: "It's hard to believe that you're going to see any serious movement before you have another Israeli government."In the meantime, the Board of Peace has been trying to reassure the Israeli public about the roadmap.The High Commissioner for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov – who led months of delicate negotiations with Hamas – gave an interview to Israel's Channel 12 just hours after Netanyahu's formal rejection of the roadmap."Its goal is to make sure that Gaza is never again a threat to Israeli security and that what happened before, [on] October 7, never happens again," he said.He said the deal takes "a step-by-step approach" meaning: "If there is verified decommissioning of weapons, that they are taken away from the factions and stored and ultimately rendered unusable, Israel then withdraws from Gaza."Ultimately, Mladenov said that nothing was being built "on the basis of trust" but on "verification."Hamas has since indicated that it still remains committed to the roadmap. It called on mediators and the Board of Peace to push for Israel to stick to the terms agreed.The Israeli prime minister has confirmed that talks with the Americans are continuing.Meanwhile heavy pressure from Washington is likely to increase.Trump is also looking at an important election this year – November's midterm elections for the US Congress. His Republican party faces the prospect of heavy losses, with petrol and grocery prices pushed up, in part due to Washington's unpopular five-month-long war in Iran.The US president's own approval rating has tumbled, and he may well demand positive developments in his peace plan for Gaza in an effort to score a much-needed foreign policy win.

schema.headline: Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word

title: The making of Auqib Nabi: Kashmir's hardships to India's Test cricket squad
description: How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketerImage source, Abid BhatImage caption, Auqib replaced Jasprit Bumrah in the squad
body: How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketerImage source, Abid BhatImage caption, Auqib replaced Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the series against Sri Lanka beginning 15 AugustByMohsin KamalCricket writer"You play with so many cricket stars. Why don't you take selfies with them?"Bilal Ahmad Dar once asked his young cousin, Auqib Nabi.Auqib smiled and replied: "One day I will reach a place where they will want to take selfies with me."Years later, that prediction has come true.On Monday, the 29-year-old all-rounder became the first cricketer from Jammu and Kashmir to earn an India Test call-up after replacing Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the two-match series against Sri Lanka, which starts on 15 August.For a region where conflict, harsh winters and limited infrastructure have long restricted sporting opportunities, Auqib's selection is being seen as a landmark moment.Raised in a small village in Baramulla district, Auqib grew up playing on local grounds with little infrastructure and few opportunities. His father, Ghulam Nabi Dar, a schoolteacher, initially wanted him to concentrate on academics and become a doctor.Image source, Abid BhatImage caption, Harsh winters and limited infrastructure have long restricted cricket in Kashmir"There was no scope in cricket. We used to think playing sport was a waste of time, so I insisted that Auqib focused on his studies," Ghulam says.But Auqib's persistence eventually changed his father's mind."After seeing his passion for cricket, I accepted it. I realised that, as a parent and a teacher, I shouldn't force him to do something he didn't want to do. I started supporting him."Auqib's childhood friend, Junaid Dar, remembers growing up in an environment where professional cricket barely seemed possible."Auqib was obsessed with cricket from childhood. I used to ask him, 'Why are you doing all this? There's no future in it.' We came from a place where there was no concept of playing sport professionally and hardly any infrastructure."To pursue his dream, Auqib regularly travelled around 70km (43 miles) to Srinagar to practise on proper cricket pitches. He did not even own a pair of spike shoes when he attended his first cricket trials.But his work ethic never changed, his cousin Bilal says."Auqib is very hardworking and consistent. He knows how to fight obstacles and make a way for himself."He would wake up early to go to the gym and then practise for the rest of the day. He did that almost every day for 10 years."Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images)Image caption, A function to fete Auqib in Kashmir - he has become a local celebrityHis breakthrough came in 2020 when he made his Ranji Trophy (India's top domestic tournament) debut for Jammu and Kashmir, taking a five-wicket haul against Jharkhand.Former India all-rounder Parvez Rasool, Jammu and Kashmir's first international cricketer and Auqib's long-time captain, says one quality always stood out."I have followed Auqib's progress for a long time, and what stands out about him is his work ethic and discipline."Success, however, did not come overnight. Auqib claimed 44 wickets during the 2024-25 Ranji Trophy season, finishing as the competition's leading fast bowler, but remained largely outside the national conversation."When you do well but don't get recognition, it hurts," his father says."But we should never lose hope. Hope is what keeps the world intact. I always believed his time would come."It did.The following season, Auqib produced one of the finest bowling campaigns in recent Ranji Trophy history, taking 60 wickets in 10 matches to finish as the tournament's leading wicket-taker and help Jammu and Kashmir win their maiden Ranji Trophy title after a wait of 67 years.Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Auqib produced one of the finest bowling campaigns in recent Ranji Trophy history, taking 60 wickets in 10 matchesThose performances earned him an 84m rupees (£730,000; $982,000) Indian Premier League (IPL) contract with Delhi Capitals. Although opportunities in the IPL were limited, his red-ball exploits had already caught the attention of India's selectors.For Rasool, Auqib's Test call-up carries significance far beyond one player."Playing Test cricket is the ultimate dream for any cricketer. It was my dream too. Seeing Auqib earn that call-up fills me with immense pride."In a way, it feels like a dream many of us in Jammu and Kashmir carried has finally been realised through him. It is a historic moment not just for Auqib and his family, but for cricket across the region."He believes Auqib's journey is remarkable not just because he reached the Indian team, but because of where he came from."Making it to the Indian team is incredibly difficult for any player, but the challenge is even greater when you come from Jammu and Kashmir. For years, we have had limited infrastructure, fewer opportunities and many obstacles that players from other parts of the country don't necessarily face."To reach this level, you need exceptional consistency, mental strength and the determination to keep believing in yourself. Auqib has shown all of those qualities, which is why this achievement is so special."Image source, Abid BhatImage caption, Auqib is also a useful lower-order batter Jammu and Kashmir became affiliated with the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) in 1957, yet the region still has only two major cricket stadiums, both with limited facilities. Long winters, heavy snowfall and decades of conflict have further slowed cricket's development."This is a landmark moment for cricket in Jammu and Kashmir," Rasool says."For a long time, people questioned whether someone from our region could make it to India's Test team. Auqib has answered that question. His selection shows players from Jammu and Kashmir can compete with the best if they are given the opportunity."He believes Auqib's journey will inspire a new generation."When I started playing, there weren't many role models from Jammu and Kashmir. Today, things are changing."Auqib becoming the first player from the region to earn an India Test call-up will give countless youngsters the belief that they can dream big too. His journey proves that no matter where you come from or what challenges you face, hard work and perseverance can take you to the highest level."Back in Baramulla, Ghulam Nabi now finds himself recognised everywhere he goes."People come up to me, hug me and say, 'This is Auqib's father.'"It makes me immensely proud."

schema.headline: The making of Auqib Nabi: Kashmir's hardships to India's Test cricket squad

title: 30 years later, a former rival will stand trial for Tupac's murder
description: It's been three decades filled with mystery, conspiracies - and anger.The drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996
body: It's been three decades filled with mystery, conspiracies - and anger.The drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 changed the trajectory of hip-hop and elevated the rapper from the face of the genre to a cultural icon.His killing became one of popular culture's great mysteries, with countless theories but no arrests until 2023, when Duane "Keffe D" Davis was unexpectedly charged with murdering the famous rapper.The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He's pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he faces life in prison without parole.The trial is likely to unravel the intricacies of the bitter and deadly East Coast vs West Coast rap rivalries and turf wars between the Bloods and the Crips street gangs that were immortalised in rap lyrics and news reports in the 1990s.It could also include several celebrity witnesses - including Suge Knight, the former CEO of Death Row Records, who has been thought of as the last surviving witness to Shakur's death.But the complicated case hinges almost exclusively on one key piece of evidence: a book co-authored by Davis that he has argued is partially a piece of fiction.Jury selection in the case began on Monday, with opening arguments due to start on 17 August.To understand how the case became so mythologised, you have to go back to rivalries that grew larger than the men at its centre.In the Los Angeles gang landscape of the 1990s, there was a vicious turf war between the Bloods, often represented by the colour red, and Crips, who often wore blue. But that territorial dispute spread through the airwaves as part of a bigger national rivalry - East Coast v West Coast rap. The genre dispute was represented by two rival record companies that defined 1990s hip-hop: Knight's Death Row Records and Sean "Diddy" Combs' Bad Boy Records. "The funny thing about it is Tupac is actually an East Coast rapper," said Jeff Pearlman, author of Only God Can Judge Me: The Many Lives of Tupac Shakur.Born in New York City, Tupac moved to northern California as a teenager. He became known as a southern California rapper after signing with Death Row Records, which included acts like Snoop Dogg and Dr Dre.Santi Elijah Holley, author of An Amerikan Family: The Shakurs and the Nation They Created, says the Death Row persona never told the whole story.Tupac's mother Afeni was a Black Panther and he grew up around the black liberation movement. Holley says his music became his politics: "His activism was his art, his lyrics."He acted in a number of Hollywood movies, and released hip-hop's first double album, All Eyez on Me, which sold over 5,000,000 copies. That album, which debuted months before his death, cemented his place in the cannon of gangsta rap, a genre that celebrated the violent life of street criminals and drug dealers.After he was shot in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996, he became immortalised as a kind of martyr for the lifestyle he helped make famous.That fatal night began when Tupac and Knight attended a boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon at the MGM Grand.After the match, surveillance footage captured Tupac and members of his entourage, who police have said were associated the Mob Piru Bloods street gang, attacking a man named Orlando Anderson, an alleged member of the South Side Compton Crips.About three hours after the attack, Tupac was riding in the passenger seat of Knight's BMW driving through Las Vegas when a white Cadillac pulled alongside them and opened fire.Tupac was hit four times and died six days later.For nearly three decades, the killing remained one of America's most famous unsolved murders. There is no single explanation why.Las Vegas police have long said witnesses refused to co-operate. Members of Tupac's entourage said police initially treated them like suspects and failed to follow important leads.Within weeks of the shooting, investigators had identified Anderson from the MGM footage and questioned him.He denied involvement and was never charged; he was killed in an unrelated shooting in 1998.Over the years, police say they pursued thousands of tips, but the case stalled amid disappearing witnesses, many of whom were also killed in gang-related shootings, limited physical evidence, and a street code that forbade co-operation with police.It was years later when Anderson's uncle, Davis, started talking and according to police, blew the case wide open again.It was ultimately the death of another legendary rapper that helped unravel Tupac's shooting death.Months after Shakur was gunned down, Biggie Smalls, or the Notorious BIG, was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles.Both rappers were the stars of their respective rival record labels - Shakur with Death Row Records and Biggie with Bad Boy Records.Biggie's case has remained unsolved, with no arrests or suspects.In the mid 2000s the Los Angeles Police Department reopened the investigation and spoke with Davis, who was at a party with Biggie before the fatal shooting. While Davis said he didn't have information about Biggie's death, he did have knowledge of Tupac's case and shared that he was in the car when the rapper was shot and killed. He told police the information in exchange that he not be charged.That deal stuck until years later, when Davis went public with his knowledge.He co-authored a memoir in 2019 titled Compton Street Legend, that claimed he not only was inside the vehicle when Tupac was shot, but he was also the person who "tossed" the gun used to kill him into the backseat of the Cadillac. He never claimed to be the person who opened fire.Davis also elaborated on the shooting to the media, detailing information to reporters in interviews.Las Vegas police said his public statements had "reinvigorated" the investigation. Over the next couple of years they spent time corroborating Davis' account and then in 2023, searched his home and seized multiple computers, two tubs of photographs and a slew of Tupac-related material, including a Vibe magazine.He was arrested later that year.Prosecutors have alleged that Tupac's killing was in retaliation for the beating of Davis' nephew - Orlando Anderson - just hours before the shooting.They claim that Davis was the architect of the crime, who ordered the shooting and supplied the deadly weapon to further gang criminal conduct.Listen to Fame Under Fire: The Tupac Murder TrialNevada prosecutors argued that by publicly talking about what happened on the night of Tupac's death and writing a book where he claimed to have supplied the gun, Davis had broken the agreement he entered into with law enforcement. A judge later sided with the prosecutor's argument, opening the door for Davis' arrest.Davis and his defence team have argued that the book was co-authored and sections were embellished or fictionalised to make a profit, and they should not be viewed as direct admissions. In an interview last week with a local TV news station, Davis denied being in Las Vegas when Tupac was killed and distanced himself from the memoir that lists him as an author."I did not write that book," Davis told Fox 5. "A ghost writer wrote that."He also said he might take the stand and testify at his trial. "If I have to, I will."Trial attorney Shaun Kent told the BBC: "This is what makes this case so fascinating. The two biggest pieces of evidence against Keffe D came from Keffe D."Keffe D has the right to take the stand and say 'I made all this up. I lied to sell copies of the book. I lied to the police. I'm a liar but I did not murder Tupac.'"Davis has also publicly stated multiple times that Bad Boy Records head Sean "Diddy" Combs had offered him $1m to kill Death Row Records rivals Tupac and Knight.

schema.headline: 30 years later, a former rival will stand trial for Tupac's murder

title: BBC asks Infantino if he will resign as Fifa president
description: The BBC has asked Fifa president Gianni Infantino if he has the support of football's South American governing body, Conmebol.The Fifa head has faced
body: The BBC has asked Fifa president Gianni Infantino if he has the support of football's South American governing body, Conmebol.The Fifa head has faced multiple calls to resign after his highly controversial attempt to sell private stakes in the World Cup, which he later abandoned.Infantino, who did not answer the BBC's questions, was in Colombia for the inauguration of the country's new President Abelardo de la Espriella.The BBC's South America correspondent Ione Wells later asked the Fifa president if he would step down.Read more: Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president

title: Watch: What we know about suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan
description: Suspected cartel leader Daniel Kinahan has appeared in front of a special non-jury court in Dublin after an extradition treaty between Ireland and the
body: Suspected cartel leader Daniel Kinahan has appeared in front of a special non-jury court in Dublin after an extradition treaty between Ireland and the UAE brought his 10 years of exile in Dubai to an abrupt end.Kinahan, aged 49, has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017. He has previously denied all charges against him.But what do we know about Daniel Kinahan, one of the most wanted men in the world, and his alleged leadership of the billion-dollar Kinahan cartel?More on this story: Suspected crime boss Kinahan spends first night in custody in Ireland

title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
description: ByTiffanie TurnbullReporting fromDryandra, Western Australia"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.Obediently, we scan the ends
body: ByTiffanie TurnbullReporting fromDryandra, Western Australia"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland – in the south-western corner of Australia – is one of the few places they remain.As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.Image source, Sharon Jones/BBCImage caption, Dryandra Woodland is one of the few places you can still find wild numbatsAustralia has long been celebrated as a nature haven, home to some of the world's most unique plant and animal species. More than 80% cannot be found anywhere else.But it has arguably become the extinction capital of the world, losing roughly four species every decade - and the decline is only worsening.Dedicated volunteers and under-funded conservationists have been slowing the army of increasing threats, but experts fear that without urgent action and political courage, the biodiversity Australia says it loves is headed for a bloodbath."It's not even a case of imagining it, it's happening in front of our own eyes," Professor Euan Ritchie tells the BBC.The many threats driving extinctionImage source, Sharon Jones/BBCImage caption, Dr Tony Friend first started working at Dryandra in the 80sIf spotting a rare creature in the wild wasn't challenging enough, the numbat is a squirrel-sized camouflage connoisseur, explains Dr Tony Friend, the godfather of conservation in the state of Western Australia."They just slept in today," jokes Rob McLean, president of the Numbat Taskforce, a volunteer group which makes a lot of Tony's thinly-resourced work possible.For two weeks each spring, as the young start venturing from their burrows, this team drives a daily circuit and records every numbat spotted. They log GPS coordinates, measure the distance to the road, and use a complicated equation to estimate the density of the animals in these woods and, from that, broader population health.One person sits in concentrated silence at each window, another perched in the back of the pick-up truck, ducking for the occasional limb branching from trees which rise around us.Through the trunks, we get the occasional glimpse of the razed farmland which tightly fences this pocket of protected woodland. On the side of one trail is a machine which detects and sprays feral cats and foxes with poison, another reminder of the perils numbats face."This year's been a bit of a feast," Rob admits.For hours on end, we cruise around, seeing parrots, wallabies, a goanna and a couple of echidnas - but no numbats.Tony arrived at Dryandra back in the 80s to find a numbat population fewer than 50. Many of the culprits then were the same as those still driving extinctions across the nation today.Image source, Courtesy WA DBCAImage caption, Feral cats kill an estimated three billion animals in Australia each yearSwathes of critical habitat are being cleared for development or industries like farming, mining and timber. Leaving a trail of destruction in their wake are introduced pests: fire ants, cane toads, rabbits, foxes, feral cats.Invasive weeds like lantana are choking the Australian bush, chlamydia has sent koalas to the edge of existence across much of the country, while the skin-eating chytrid fungus has caused seven frog extinctions here and counting.The changing climate is creating unliveable conditions for some species, like native flying foxes which are dropping out of trees in their thousands due to extreme temperatures. For others it is eliminating their food or their homes.Climate change is also driving natural disasters which fry and drown both plants and animals with now frightening regularity. The infamous Black Summer bushfires of 2019-20, for example, killed an estimated three billion animals. The successive years of record-breaking flooding which followed were so widespread it's impossible to estimate the impact on wildlife.Image source, Sharon Jones/BBCImage caption, The Carnaby's black cockatoo is another species barely hanging on in south-western Australia Many species once abundant across the continent are now isolated to increasingly small and disjointed patches, each impact compounding and leaving them more vulnerable to the next.There are small, yet determined, efforts to slow the momentum of decline.As a young numbat scoffs his breakfast – custard with "termite sprinkles" – at Perth Zoo, a keeper explains how this stud's upcoming release at Dryandra will help boost genetic diversity."When you get that feedback: your babies have got babies, it's very satisfying," Vicki Power says.Breeding programmes like this have also made setting up additional populations of an array of threatened species possible.But many cannot survive in the true wild, where large-scale predator control remains an endless battle, and are instead sent to fenced nature reserves, themselves high-maintenance undertakings facing problems like in-breeding and overpopulation.Habitat protection or restoration projects have been ramping up, but they are not keeping pace with destruction, particularly in the most critical areas.Scientists are also trying to fight disease, though that's an expensive and laborious endeavour, which for most species buys only a little more time. Others are preserving genetic material in case we ever work out how to resurrect species from the dead.A hundred species lost - and countingScientists agree that we're living though the world's sixth mass extinction event, the first caused by humans. But Australia is at the front of this trend.It leads the world in mammal extinctions, and medals when it comes to the loss of other species classes too."Despite Australia being one of the wealthiest countries per capita in the world and having more than its fair share of world-leading scientists… we have a truly awful record of conserving species," Ritchie says."And things aren't getting better."The Australian government's official extinctions list sits at 67, but researchers are confident at least 100 plant and animal species have been lost forever.They suspect the true figure is far higher. The country is still discovering species which have already been wiped out.Though the rate of extinction in Australia has stayed stable, at around four per decade, the number of threatened species is still climbing quickly, and the deterioration of many is only gathering speed.This trajectory has some scary flow-on effects, experts warn. Australia's biodiversity "underpins everything", ecologist Jack Pascoe says.Think food production, tourism, construction – much of the economy. Potential scientific breakthroughs could be stymied: in medicine, agriculture and even climate change adaptation. And for First Nations Australians, the decline also threatens their culture."We think of ourselves as custodians of all life on Earth… so there's a much more personal and social feeling of loss that comes when these things are not doing well or we lose them forever," Pascoe, a man from the Yuin Aboriginal nation, says.Decades of failuresThough environment protection is a state responsibility, the federal government oversees matters of national importance.Labor took office in 2022, promising no new extinctions under its watch, and it has sought to make nature protection a defining feature of its second term."It's well understood that nature is facing many challenges in the world today, both here in Australia, and overseas… we are losing biodiversity at an alarming rate," Environment Minister Murray Watt told the BBC in a statement.His party has significantly increased Australia's emissions reduction efforts and massively boosted renewable energy projects. There is some praise for their work on drawing critically endangered mammals back from the brink. And the passage of revamped environment laws last year was heralded as the most significant reform in a generation.The country also has an ambitious goal to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.But there's limited optimism that this will be a real turning point.The new laws are only the scaffolding of change. The substance of it is still being worked out – in the form of National Environmental Standards (NES) and a federal watchdog to enforce them.And many in the sector say the problem is not so much the regulatory tools available, but rather the political will to use them.Successive governments have failed to adequately protect the environment over the past 30 years, Australia's longest serving environment minister tells the BBC.​​That includes his own administration. "We should have done more too," says Robert Hill, who lead the last major reforms in 1999 under John Howard's conservative coalition.Image source, Courtesy Perth ZooImage caption, Vicki Power and Tony Friend have spent decades trying to save the numbatMany of the challenges of his era still haunt leaders today.The nation's wealth has largely been built off the back of its natural resources – often at the expense of the environment. Those riches still underpin the economy and help fund government spending on essentials like healthcare and housing.Then there's the added pressure applied by industry and the competing interests of states - whose stake in regulatory controls blurs the lines of accountability and increases bureaucratic hurdles.These battles leave even the toughest environmental advocates within governments bruised.For example, the Albanese government last year rushed through laws protecting salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officials, silencing opposition from within and ignoring advice from its own department concerning the impact of the A$1.4bn (£733m; $989m) industry on the survival of the Maugean Skate, an endangered ray."The axe falls on the environmental outcome if there's the alternative of an economic one," Hill says."Even if [the federal government] does want to act, it's still got to have the political strength to turn its aspirations into reality."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Albanese government passed legislation to protect salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officialsThere is also a belief that greater regulation alone will achieve little.Too much conservation work currently relies on philanthropists' cash and devoted volunteers, those in the sector say, and much more languishes on the to-do list due to a lack of money.The federal government directly spends about A$700m on nature protection, a fraction of the A$33bn – or 1% of GDP – conservationists say it should be. That is an eyebrow-raising figure, people like Paul Elton concede, but one they argue is reasonable.According to his research – which the government disputes – more than A$26bn is still being spent on subsidies for things like mining, intensive agriculture or fuel despite Australia signing global pledges to wind them back."For every dollar the government is spending on positive biodiversity conservation action, there's A$26 being spent on subsidies that are causing harm to nature," he tells the BBC."That's a pretty stark imbalance."Minister Watt didn't directly respond to questions about conservationists' demands, but said: "We remain committed to long-term environmental recovery, in partnership with state and local governments, community and environmental groups."Though public sentiment is shifting, there's scepticism the government will prioritise the environment amid competing demands and compounding crises until voters force them to do so."The community will say to you, we should spend a lot of money on the environment. And then if you say, 'Well, what are you prepared to sacrifice to ensure that funding base?', then they're no longer interested," Hill says.In the face of so many challenges and what they see as little progress, advocates admit it's hard to hang on to hope."We know what the problems are. We know how to address them. We know when we spend money on the environment, it pays back many times over," Ritchie, a mammal ecologist, says."It's like being a doctor and seeing all these sick people in the community and you know how to fix them, but no one will let you do that."Image source, Sharon Jones/BBCImage caption, Volunteer 'Jacko' keeps watch from the back of the truckSmall wins, like the future of the numbat, keep them fighting.There are now around 3,000 nationwide, and in Dryandra numbers have increased ten-fold. The animal has recently been taken off the international endangered species list and is now classified as near-threatened.It takes five hours, but finally synchronised cries of excitement come from the driver's seat and the back of the pick-up truck. The cause of the commotion stands frozen and alert at the end of a hollowing log."It's not a competition," Rob says. Chuckling, he points at his rival spotter: "But I beat him by a second."The dam has broken. Over the next little while we see eight numbats, including two pairs of babies, blinking at us in the dusky light.This year's full count, Tony later tells me, is one of the best yet."But I remind people they're not out of the woods yet," Tony says.The relief at the numbat's revival is tempered by worry this will make it harder to access the funding and support needed to cement those gains.The woylie, or brush-tailed bettong, is a cautionary tale. It recovered slightly and was taken off the threatened list only to be added again a decade later, in a worse state."We can't walk away," Tony says, "and say 'no, they're fine,' you know?""It's got to be accepted that continued work is needed to keep that animal on the planet."AsiaAustraliaWildlifeWildlife conservation

schema.headline: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope

title: Moment opposition MP throws eggs at prime minister of Kosovo

body: An opposition MP, Time Kadrijaj, threw eggs at Kosovo's acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti during a plenary session on Saturday. The Alliance party MP hurled at least four eggs in Kurti's direction before lawmakers and police officers intervened. Chaos unfolded after Kurti told Parliament he needed more time to hold talks with other parties before proposing a candidate for speaker following the June snap election.

title: Kinahan: How his hearing unfolded inside the courtroom in Dublin
description: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appeared in court in Dublin on Sunday after being extradited from Dubai following his arrest there in April. Kinah
body: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appeared in court in Dublin on Sunday after being extradited from Dubai following his arrest there in April. Kinahan has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017. The 49-year-old was remanded in custody after appearing at the non-jury Special Criminal Court in Dublin, telling the court: " I think we all know I won't be getting bail." The Kinahan cartel has been responsible for trafficking tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world for more than 20 years, according to the UK's National Crime Agency. The BBC's Ireland correspondent, Chris Page, was inside the court during the hearing.More on this story.

title: New train service connects Finland and Sweden for first time in decades
description: Finland uses the same track widths as Russia, which are wider than the European standard - a holdover from when the Nordic nation was part of the Russ
body: Finland uses the same track widths as Russia, which are wider than the European standard - a holdover from when the Nordic nation was part of the Russian Grand Duchy in the 19th and early 20th centuries.It is currently in the process of updating its track widths to match the European standard.The new, twice-daily journey to Sweden's Haparanda takes 100-minutes as it hugs the west coast of Finland before crossing the border between the two Nordic neighbours.Passengers travelling on from Haparanda will need to transfer onto a different train to continue southward.But the service makes it possible to travel around 5,000km by rail from Portugal's Algarve to Finland's northernmost train station of Kolari - believed to be the longest train route in Europe.It will also enable a 24-hour train journey between capitals Helsinki and Stockholm.Finland's transport minister said the return of the cross-border service shows cooperation between the two countries was growing "all the time".Elisa Markula, chief executive of Finland's state-owned railway operator VR, said she hopes the service will benefit from a "renaissance" in rail travel across Europe."Train travelling in all Europe is having a renaissance. Also in Finland, our passenger numbers are increasing a lot," Markula told AFP.

schema.headline: New train service connects Finland and Sweden for first time in decades
